title: Instagram Rolls Out Anti‑Creeper Feature, Sparking Mass Quit Pledges Across the Platform
body:
Instagram has rolled out a paid subscription called “Instagram Plus,” a $3.99‑a‑month tier that promises users more expressive tools and deeper connections. The move, however, has sparked a backlash among privacy‑concerned members of the platform, who argue that the new service effectively ends the veil of anonymity that many “stalkers” have relied on. Within hours of the announcement, a wave of comments on social media warned, “If you have Instagram Plus, stay away from me,” while others vowed to delete the app altogether.

The premium offering bundles a suite of enhancements that Instagram says will let creators showcase their work in richer formats, access exclusive stickers, and enjoy an ad‑free experience. But the headline feature that has ignited the controversy is a redesign of the “view‑only” profile mode. Previously, users could browse a public profile without leaving a trace—no “seen” indicator, no record of who had visited. Instagram Plus removes that cloak, automatically logging every profile visit in a new “Recent Viewers” section visible to the profile owner. The change is marketed as a way to foster genuine interaction, but critics say it turns casual browsing into a surveillance tool.

Privacy advocates point out that the shift undermines a long‑standing, albeit informal, norm on the platform. “People have used the ability to view profiles anonymously as a safety net,” said Dr. Lena Ortiz, a digital‑rights researcher at the Center for Online Integrity. “Now the moment you look at someone’s feed, they’ll know. That’s a fundamental alteration of user expectations, and it feels like a step toward coercive engagement.” The concern is especially acute for individuals who monitor public figures, journalists, or potential romantic interests without wanting to reveal their interest. For them, the new feature could expose personal curiosity and make them vulnerable to unwanted attention or retaliation.

The backlash is not limited to privacy‑focused users. Several high‑profile creators have expressed unease about the subscription model itself. While Instagram touts the tier as a way to empower creators with more monetisation tools, many argue that the $3.99 fee is a barrier for smaller accounts that rely on organic growth. “We already pay for ads and analytics,” said Maya Patel, a lifestyle influencer with 120,000 followers. “Now we’re being asked to pay again for something that feels like a gimmick. It’s a cash‑grab that could widen the gap between big brands and everyday creators.” The sentiment echoes broader industry criticism that social‑media giants are increasingly layering paid features on top of free services, turning basic functionality into a premium commodity.

From a business perspective, Instagram’s move aligns with Meta’s broader strategy to diversify revenue beyond advertising. The company has been experimenting with subscription models across its family of apps, including a paid version of Facebook and a premium tier for WhatsApp. Industry analysts see Instagram Plus as a test case to gauge user willingness to pay for enhanced experiences while also gathering more data on engagement patterns. “If the subscription sticks, it could unlock a new revenue stream that’s less volatile than ad spend,” noted tech analyst Rajiv Menon of MarketPulse. “But the risk is alienating a user base that’s already fatigued by constant feature churn and privacy concerns.”

The immediate fallout includes a surge in posts warning friends and followers about the new “view‑tracker” and a noticeable uptick in account deletions reported by third‑party monitoring tools. Instagram has responded with a brief FAQ, emphasizing that the viewer log is optional and can be disabled in settings, but the clarification arrived after the initial wave of criticism. The company has also promised a trial period for existing users before the feature becomes mandatory for all Plus subscribers.

Looking ahead, the success of Instagram Plus will likely hinge on how Meta balances monetisation with user trust. If the platform can demonstrate tangible benefits—such as meaningful analytics for creators or genuinely ad‑free browsing—some users may accept the price tag. However, the perception that the service erodes privacy could drive a segment of the community toward alternative apps that champion anonymity. As social media continues to evolve into a paid ecosystem, the debate sparked by Instagram’s latest rollout may serve as a bellwether for how much users are willing to sacrifice in exchange for convenience and self‑expression.
